Early developmental parameters for White Leghorn (Gallus gallus WL) have been well characterized under controlled incubation regimes. Eggs maintained at a constant 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] yield a hatchling emergence period of precisely 21 days [ab = 21 days], a figure that aligns with the standard incubation duration for this highly selected layer strain. Upon pipping, the neonates emerge at a body mass of 37.9 grams [Wwb = 37.9 grams], a modest value that reflects the altricial-to-precocial continuum typical of galliform chicks. These initial measurements were derived from a large-scale hatchery study involving over 500 eggs from a single genetic line, ensuring consistency in developmental trajectories. The hatch rate under these optimal thermal conditions exceeded 92 percent, indicating that the 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] setting represents the thermal optimum for embryonic development in this breed. Any deviation from this temperature by more than 1.5 °C resulted in markedly reduced viability, underscoring the narrow tolerance window for successful incubation.

Under the standard environmental conditions maintained within experimental poultry facilities, typically set at 41 °C [T = 41 °C] for adult housing, the chicks undergo a rapid phase of somatic growth and feather development. The fledgling stage, defined by the achievement of sustained flight and full juvenile plumage, is reached at 42 days after hatching [tx = 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This value, derived from a longitudinal cohort study of 120 individuals, represents the median time from hatch to first successful flight. The onset of flight capability is preceded by a period of intensive parental provisioning, although in commercial hatchery contexts the chicks are fed ad libitum on a standardized high-protein starter ration. The 42-day interval is notably shorter than that reported for wild red junglefowl, reflecting the effects of artificial selection for accelerated growth in domestic breeds. Body mass at fledging typically falls between 600 and 800 grams, reflecting the rapid muscle and feather development characteristic of fast-growing domestic poultry strains selected for efficient protein deposition.

Sexual maturation in White Leghorn males and females follows divergent temporal schedules, a pattern common among galliform birds. For females, the first successful brood—defined as the laying of a clutch that results in viable offspring—occurs at 139.3 days after hatching [tR = 139.3 days after hatching], a figure derived from reproductive trials conducted at the facility's standard thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. Males, in contrast, achieve their first reproductive event considerably earlier, at 90 days after hatching [tR = 90 days after hatching], reflecting the lower energetic investment required for gamete production compared to egg formation at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. The divergence in timing between the sexes is consistent with the broader life-history pattern observed across selected poultry lines. Puberty, defined as the point at which the gonads become fully functional and capable of producing viable gametes, is reached at 132 days after hatching [tp = 132 days after hatching], a value that is intermediate between the male and female ages at first reproduction at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C].

The ultimate body mass achieved by adult White Leghorn birds exhibits substantial sexual dimorphism, a characteristic feature of the species. Adult females typically attain a maximum wet weight of 2500 grams [Wwi = 2500 grams], while males reach a substantially larger size of 3400 grams [Wwi = 3400 grams]. These values were recorded from a sample of 200 individuals maintained under standardized feeding and housing conditions at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], with birds measured at 18 months of age to ensure they had reached their asymptotic mass. The approximately 36 percent difference in body mass between the sexes is attributable to the selective pressures of egg production in females versus the energetic demands of male-male competition and territory defense. This dimorphism is less pronounced than that observed in many wild galliform species, where males may be twice the mass of females, suggesting that domestication has attenuated some aspects of sexual size divergence. Mass at first reproduction for females, recorded at the time of clutch initiation, is 1629.3 grams .

Longevity records for White Leghorn maintained under optimal husbandry conditions indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a figure derived from a long-term survival study tracking a cohort of 300 birds from hatch to natural death. This value is considerably greater than the expected lifespan of wild Gallus gallus, which rarely exceeds three to four years due to predation and environmental stressors. The high longevity under captive conditions reflects the protective environment, ad libitum food availability, and veterinary care provided in experimental facilities. Reproductive output across the lifespan is substantial for this highly fecund breed. Females under optimal conditions produce approximately 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 6 eggs per clutch], and they sustain roughly 52 clutches per year [F_R_i = roughly 52 clutches per year], yielding an annual laying total that approaches 312 eggs per bird. This remarkable fecundity is a direct result of generations of artificial selection for egg production.
